turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm glad you came in. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, Doc... I’m really only here because everybody keeps acting like I’m imagining the whole thing. My wife, my family, they all look at me like I'm just making this up or losing my grip, but I know what I know. I know for an absolute fact that my wife’s relative has been coming into this house just to get at me. 

I mean, I work as a fabricator, right? I’ve been assembling parts and working with my hands my whole life. I am a very organized guy. I know exactly where I leave my equipment. But I'll go out to my garage, and my things are shifted around. My tools don’t just move themselves. A socket wrench doesn't just sprout legs and walk across the workbench, you know? But everyone just says, "Oh, you just misplaced it, you're getting older." No, I didn't misplace a thing. 

And it’s not just the garage, either. Every single weekend—and I mean every weekend without fail—my fishing plans get completely spoiled by some "accident." My gear is messed with, the line is tangled up, or something is suddenly wrong with the truck. That is not a coincidence. After all these months of this happening, day in and day out, I can see plain as day what's going on. He’s been trying to take over my place. He wants to push me out of my own home, just edge me right out of the picture entirely, and nobody wants to listen to me about it. They just sit there and tell me I'm crazy, but I'm the one living it.

turns.doctor_question: How certain are you that this is really happening, if at all?

If you walked into your office here, right, and your pens were moved from the left side of your desk to the right, and your chair was lowered three inches, and your files were out of alphabetical order, would you just say, 'Oh, well, I guess I'm just losing my mind'? No, you'd know someone had been in here. 

That's exactly what I'm dealing with. I have been an assembler for thirty-two years. Thirty-two years of putting things together, exactly where they belong, piece by piece. My brain works like a blueprint. I don't misplace a 5/8 inch wrench. I don't accidentally leave the chuck key out of the drill press. But I go out there, and it's moved. And my wife's relative—he was over here for Thanksgiving, right? And ever since then, it's been this slow, methodical campaign. 

It’s not just the garage, like I said. It’s the fishing gear. Every Saturday morning, I wake up at 4:30 AM. I make my coffee—black, no sugar—and I go out to load the truck. And every single time, without fail, something is wrong. Last week, the spark plug wires on my outboard motor were swapped. Swapped! You don't just accidentally swap spark plug wires. Two weeks before that, someone had let exactly ten pounds of air out of my front left tire. Just enough to be a problem, not enough to be obvious right away. 

And my wife, she just sighs and rolls her eyes and tells me I'm being paranoid. But I see what he's doing. It's so clear to me. He wants to make me look incompetent. He wants her to think I'm losing it, so he can step in, be the man of the house, and push me right out the door. I’ve seen the way he looks around my property, sizing it up. I know it sounds crazy to you, and I know it sounds crazy to my family, but I am living it every single day. I am as certain of this as I am that the sun is going to come up tomorrow morning. There is no 'if at all' about it. It is happening.

It is physically sitting there. Anyone could see it if they just bothered to actually look! If my wife walked out there and actually looked at the pegboard instead of just rolling her eyes, she would see it too. But she doesn't. 

In my line of work—fabrication, assembling—you have to trust your eyes and your ears. If a machine has a bad bearing, you hear the rattle. It's a real sound. If a piece of sheet metal is cut a sixteenth of an inch off, you see it. You don't imagine it, it's just a fact of the material. And that's how I operate. I deal in hard facts. So when I look under the hood of my truck and see the spark plug wires swapped, I am looking at real rubber and real wire. I can touch them. I can hold them in my hands. 

I don't hear things other people don't hear. I hear my wife sighing at me. I hear the neighbor's dog barking. I hear real things. And I see real things. I see that relative of hers sizing up my living room. I see the tire on my truck sitting a little lower because exactly ten pounds of air is gone. It’s all real, physical evidence, Doc. So no, I'm not making things up in my head. Everything I'm dealing with is happening right here in the real world, in broad daylight. It's just that I'm the only one willing to actually open my eyes and look at the evidence.

So no, I'm not bouncing off the walls or staying up all night doing jumping jacks. I need my sleep. You can't be sleep-deprived around industrial equipment, or you'll end up losing a finger, or worse. I usually try to be in bed, boots off, lights out, by 10:00 PM sharp.

That's just the reality of having to constantly be on guard in your own home because someone is actively trying to dismantle your life piece by piece while everyone else looks the other way. I want to sleep. I want to just close my eyes and rest like a normal guy. I definitely don't have any extra energy to spare, I can promise you that much.
